title: Shuttle Imaging Radar B Launches aboard STS-41-G
description: Launch of the second flight of Shuttle Imaging Radar aboard the Space Shuttle. Using radar pulses rather than optical light, imaging radar can "see" through desert sands, for example, to detect the remnants of ancient riverbeds. Earth was mapped from approximately 60° N latitude to 60° S latitude.

transcript.text: JPL's shuttle imaging radar is scheduled to make its second flight aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Challenger this fall.
The experiment is called CERB for short.
It will study Earth's ocean and land surfaces from the open payload bay of the Challenger.
The radar first flew as CERA in 1981 aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia.
Results of that experiment showed that the shuttle is a valuable platform for viewing the Earth with imaging radar.
What we found out is that if we have a dry environment, then the radar can penetrate about 1 to 6 meters through a sand layer
and basically image the features which are below that sand layer.
The main difference on the antenna of CERB is that it will be foldable and deployable and it's larger than the CERA
and basically is a configuration of it at launch. It will be configured in this arrangement.
Once we get in orbit, the sand antenna panels will be opened which will take about 1 minute operation to open the antennas.
And then after that we can operate in the radiator toward the Earth.
In addition, during specific data take, we'll be moving the antenna so we can illuminate the surface at a variety of angles
instead of as a fixed angle which was the case in the CERA experiment.
Unlike passive camera systems that record only the sunlight reflected from Earth's surface,
imaging radar illuminates its own target by transmitting millions of microwave radar pulses sequentially along a broad swath.
The signal bounces back to the shuttle and the unique signature of each reflected pulse is recorded by the radar.
These millions of radar snapshots are then reconstructed by computers to produce detailed black and white images of the Earth's surface.
